CENTRAL FOCUS
Historical Spine and Essential Distinctions
[1] Liberalism emerged historically in the West to attack feudal privilege and create
space for the entrepreneurial class against authoritarian rule (Gauba, PDF p.40).
v
[2] Its core tenets include rational individuality, natural rights, consent, civil
society and state as artificial institutions, primacy of fair procedure, civil.
v
[3] In its early classical phase, Locke, Smith and Bentham defend laissez-faire and the
negative role of the state; the state is treated as a necessary evil and the.
v
[4] Mill and then Green, Hobhouse, Laski and Tawney move liberalism toward welfare and
positive state action to secure a dignified life (Gauba, PDF p.41).
v

panels.panel_title: Thinkers, Illustrations and the Comparison Matrix
lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
Thinkers, Illustrations and the Comparison Matrix
[1] A classical liberal state protects life, property and contract and avoids broad
interference in production and exchange (Gauba, PDF p.41).
v
[2] A welfare liberal state taxes and regulates in order to provide education, health
and social security, because dignity requires more than non-interference alone.
v
[3] A neoliberal response says forced transfer of resources harms liberty and that
markets coordinate needs better than governments can (Gauba, PDF pp.42-43).
v

panels.panel_title: Classical, New, Welfare-State and Neoliberal Strands
lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
Classical, New, Welfare-State and Neoliberal Strands
[1] Liberalism puts individual liberty at the centre of public policy and opposes
arbitrary authority (Gauba, PDF p.40).
v
[2] Its core vocabulary includes rights, consent, procedure, civil liberties, contract
and rule-limited government (Gauba, PDF pp.40-41, 45).
v
[3] Classical liberalism is laissez-faire and negative-state; welfare liberalism is
positive-state; neoliberalism is rollback liberalism (Gauba, PDF pp.41-43).
v
[4] Gauba's critique focuses on bourgeois bias, unequal group power and the gap between
market liberty and actual social welfare (Gauba, PDF pp.43-44).
v
SYNTHESIS -> Classical, New, Welfare-State and Neoliberal Strands is best presented through
its central claim, causal logic, strongest limit and qualified verdict.
EXAM ROUTE -> define precisely -> explain the mechanism -> test the limit ->
conclude with a qualified political judgment.

panels.panel_title: Hayek and Nozick: Different Routes to the Minimal State
lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
Hayek and Nozick: Different Routes to the Minimal State
[1] Knowledge argument: neoliberalism holds that governments cannot possess sufficient
knowledge of dispersed individual needs and circumstances to plan an economy.
v
[2] Price/market-coordination argument: the neoliberal claim is that decentralized
market exchange coordinates dispersed knowledge and choices more effectively than.
v
[3] Coercion argument: on this view, forced or compulsory redistribution (tax-financed
welfare, state intervention) is itself a form of coercion that curtails freedom.
v
